title: About
text:
Hi, I’m Hui Yao (姚惠) — a ScM student in Biostatistics at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
I am broadly interested in survival analysis, reproducible statistical workflows, and wearable / sensor-based health data. My current work includes building simulation pipelines to benchmark methods for reconstructing individual patient data (IPD) from Kaplan–Meier curves, with a focus on different censoring mechanisms, proportional vs non-proportional hazards, and robust evaluation metrics.
Before joining Johns Hopkins, I completed my BSc in Statistics at the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) in Shenzhen, China, and spent a semester as a fully funded exchange student at the University of Notre Dame, where I deepened my training in numerical analysis, computational statistics, and data mining.

title: About
text:
Applied research & internships

UNFPA Ecuador (United Nations Population Fund) – Data Analysis & Research Assistant
Led small-area estimation of child malnutrition at the cantonal level using census, survey, and administrative data, and helped build a reproducible R-based workflow and Power BI dashboard for UN agencies and local government.
Peking University Hospital in Shenzhen – Biostatistics Division
Supported clinical collaborators with study design and data analysis, including t-tests, chi-squared tests, mediation and structural equation modeling, and wrote practical documentation for routine data workflows.
Gait and wearable data research (Prof. Jian Qing Shi’s group)
Worked on multimodal datasets (gait, EEG, clinical scales) for early screening of neurodegenerative diseases, developed feature extraction pipelines and predictive models, and collaborated with hospitals and industry partners.
Parkinson’s disease motion data & iGEM project
Built feature computation scripts and classification models for sensor-based movement data; contributed ODE-based modeling and simulation for a synthetic biology project on Tyrian purple production.

title: Example Analysis: Statistical Performance Indicators
text:
The SPI data used here originate from the World Bank [Bank (2023)], and are accessed via the TidyTuesday dataset curated by Nicola Rennie and the R4DS community [Rennie and community (2025)].

Background
The Statistical Performance Indicators (SPI), developed by the World Bank, provide a quantitative assessment of how well national statistical systems perform across five dimensions: 1. Data use 2. Data services 3. Data products 4. Data sources 5. Data infrastructure
The SPI covers nearly all countries worldwide (≈ 99% of the global population) and spans 2004–2023. It serves as a diagnostic tool to strengthen national data systems.






Note



Purpose: To monitor and improve national statistical systems’ capacity and performance.



library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

spi <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-12-02/spi_indicators.csv")

glimpse(spi)

Rows: 4,340
Columns: 12
$ iso3c                     <chr> "DNK", "FIN", "POL", "SWE", "ESP", "NLD", "S…
$ country                   <chr> "Denmark", "Finland", "Poland", "Sweden", "S…
$ region                    <chr> "Europe & Central Asia", "Europe & Central A…
$ income                    <chr> "High income", "High income", "High income",…
$ year                      <dbl> 2023, 2023, 2023, 2023, 2023, 2023, 2023, 20…
$ population                <dbl> 5946952, 5584264, 36685849, 10536632, 483733…
$ overall_score             <dbl> 95.25583, 95.11542, 94.65375, 94.41000, 94.3…
$ data_use_score            <dbl> 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100,…
$ data_services_score       <dbl> 98.46667, 96.43333, 97.30000, 96.00000, 91.2…
$ data_products_score       <dbl> 90.71250, 90.96875, 84.54375, 90.57500, 92.6…
$ data_sources_score        <dbl> 87.100, 88.175, 91.425, 85.475, 87.800, 83.6…
$ data_infrastructure_score <dbl> 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100,…




Key Questions
1.  How has a country’s statistical performance changed over time?
2.  Is statistical performance related to income level or population size?
3.  Which pillar do countries score lowest in?


Small differences in SPI between countries may reflect data imprecision rather than true performance gaps.


Data Wrangling
We clean and simplify the dataset to focus on major regions and income levels.

spi_clean <- spi |>
  filter(!is.na(overall_score)) |>
  mutate(
    income = fct_relevel(income, "Low income", "Lower middle income",
                         "Upper middle income", "High income"),
    region = fct_lump(region, n = 6)
  ) |>
  group_by(region, income, year) |>
  summarise(
    mean_spi = mean(overall_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )



Trend in Statistical Performance

ggplot(spi_clean, aes(x = year, y = mean_spi, color = income)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ region, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Trends in Statistical Performance by Income and Region",
    subtitle = "World Bank SPI 2004–2023",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Overall SPI Score",
    color = "Income Level",
    caption = "Data source: World Bank SPI, via TidyTuesday 2025-12-02"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.











Relationship with Population Size
We explore whether countries with larger populations have higher or lower SPI.

spi_recent <- spi |>
  filter(year == 2023, !is.na(population), !is.na(overall_score))

ggplot(spi_recent, aes(x = population, y = overall_score, color = income)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(
  labels = scales::label_number(
    scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()
  )
) +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Performance vs. Population Size (2023)",
    x = "Population (log scale)",
    y = "Overall SPI Score",
    caption = "Each point = one country"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










Which Pillar Scores Lowest?
We calculate the average score per pillar across all countries in 2023.

spi_pillars <- spi_recent |>
  summarise(
    data_use = mean(data_use_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    data_services = mean(data_services_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    data_products = mean(data_products_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    data_sources = mean(data_sources_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    data_infra = mean(data_infrastructure_score, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "pillar", values_to = "score")

ggplot(spi_pillars, aes(x = reorder(pillar, score), y = score, fill = pillar)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Average SPI Pillar Scores (2023)",
    x = "Pillar",
    y = "Average Score",
    caption = "Data: World Bank SPI 2023"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")










Summary
The SPI data reveal consistent improvement in statistical performance across all regions since 2004, particularly in high-income countries. However, data infrastructure and data sources pillars remain relatively weak compared with data use or services. Population size shows no strong correlation with SPI — suggesting that institutional quality matters more than scale. Future research could link SPI trends with governance or digital infrastructure indicators.


Function checklist
•   dplyr: filter(), mutate(), group_by(), summarise(), fct_relevel()
•   tidyr: pivot_longer()
•   ggplot2: geom_line(), geom_point(), geom_col(), facet_wrap()








Reference

Bank, World. 2023. “Statistical Performance Indicators (SPI).” https://datatopics.worldbank.org/statistical-performance-indicators/.


Rennie, Nicola, and R4DS TidyTuesday community. 2025. “TidyTuesday: Statistical Performance Indicators Dataset.” https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday.
